extracted.intended_audience: jurors in U.S. federal patent infringement trials (and litigants/judges using jury instructions)
extracted.subtask_description: Model/standard jury instructions explaining what a patent is, how patents are obtained, claim construction, infringement and invalidity standards, burdens/standards of proof, and related trial procedures in a U.S. federal patent infringement case.

rubrics_metrics.name: What a patent is and the rights it grants
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid United States patent gives the patent holder the right [for up to 20 years from the date the patent application was filed] [for 17 years from the date the patent issued] to prevent others from making, using, offering to sell, or selling the patented invention within the United States, or from importing it into the United States, without the patent holder’s permission. A violation of the patent holder’s rights is called infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents are granted by the PTO; they can be enforced by a federal lawsuit. The instructions explain the basic consequence of a patent grant (exclusive right to exclude) and the temporal scope indicated by filing- or issue-based terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification requirement (written description of the invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: The application includes what is called a “specification,” which contains a written description of the claimed invention telling what the invention is, how it works, how to make it, and how to use it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification concludes with one or more numbered sentences (the claims). The specification must adequately describe the invention; later instructions address written description and enablement requirements in more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define the boundaries of protection
rubrics_metrics.description: When the patent is eventually granted by the PTO, the claims define the boundaries of its protection and give notice to the public of those boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures and text in the rest of the patent provide description and context, but it is the claims that define the breadth of the patent’s coverage. Each claim is effectively treated as if it were a separate patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution process and prosecution history
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of obtaining a patent is called patent prosecution. After the applicant files the application, an Examiner reviews the application and informs the applicant in writing of whether the Examiner considers any claim to be patentable (an 'Office Action'). The papers generated during these communications between the Examiner and the applicant are called the 'prosecution history.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Examiner rejects claims the applicant may respond, change claims, or submit new claims; the process may continue and sometimes involves appeals within the PTO or to a court. The PTO's grant does not necessarily preclude a court from finding a claim invalid based on additional prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art (general definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art is information that demonstrates the state of technology that existed before the claimed invention was made or before the application was filed. The PTO searches for and reviews information that is publicly available or submitted by the applicant; this information is called 'prior art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent lists the prior art the Examiner considered (the 'cited references'). The instructions note that specific legal definitions of prior art will be provided later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement is assessed claim-by-claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement is assessed on a claim-by-claim basis. Therefore, there may be infringement as to one claim but not infringement as to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent may be infringed by making, using, selling, offering for sale, or importing a product or by using a method meeting all the requirements of a claim. Indirect forms include contributory infringement and inducement; detailed requirements for each type are provided later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (invalidity for not being new)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claim to be invalid because it is not new, [alleged infringer] must show, by clear and convincing evidence, that all of the elements of a claim are present in a single previous device or sufficiently described in a single previous printed publication or patent. We call these 'prior art.' If a claim is not new, it is said to be anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets the standard and burden for anticipation—clear and convincing evidence that a single prior-art reference discloses every claim element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness (invalidity for being obvious)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be invalid if it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the field of technology of the patent at the relevant time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if every element is not shown in a single prior-art reference, a claim may be invalid as obvious in view of the state of the art; jurors will be provided a series of questions to decide obviousness in more detail later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement (Section 112)
rubrics_metrics.description: To meet the written description requirement, the description of the invention in the specification portion of the patent must be detailed enough to demonstrate that the applicant actually possessed the invention as broadly as claimed in the claims of the issued patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a ground for invalidity where asserted; the instructions indicate that written description is a separate consideration under Section 112.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (Section 112)
rubrics_metrics.description: To meet the enablement requirement, the description in the patent has to be sufficiently full and clear to have allowed persons of ordinary skill in the field of technology of the patent to make and use the invention without undue experimentation, at the time the patent application was originally filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement and written description are distinct but related Section 112 requirements; the jury is instructed on these when such defenses are presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages aim and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A damages award should put [patent holder] in approximately the same financial position that it would have been in had the infringement not occurred, but in no event may the damages award be less than what [patent holder] would have received had it been paid a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages are compensatory, not punitive; jurors may not include additional amounts to punish the alleged infringer. The court will later instruct on the meaning and calculation of a reasonable royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willfulness determination separate from damages
rubrics_metrics.description: You will need to make a finding as to whether the infringement was willful. If you decide that any infringement was willful, that decision should not affect any damages award you give. I will take willfulness into account later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The instruction notes that willfulness may be a separate finding (sometimes requiring clear and convincing evidence) and that jurors should not adjust damages as a punishment for willfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of proof: preponderance vs clear and convincing
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two standards of proof: preponderance of the evidence ('more likely true than not') and clear and convincing evidence ('you have been left with a clear conviction that the fact has been proven').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear and convincing is a higher standard than preponderance but lower than beyond a reasonable doubt. The instruction identifies which issues use which standard (e.g., infringement is by preponderance; invalidity by clear and convincing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and meaning of claim language (claim elements/limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim sets forth, in words, a set of requirements. Each claim sets forth its requirements in a single sentence. If a device or a method satisfies each of these requirements, then it is covered by the claim. The requirements of a claim are often referred to as 'claim elements' or 'claim limitations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the meaning of the words in a claim and that they set forth the requirements is necessary to decide infringement and invalidity issues; the court defines certain terms and the jury must apply those definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent and dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'independent claim' sets forth all of the requirements that must be met in order to be covered by that claim. A 'dependent claim' refers to another claim for some of its requirements and incorporates all of the requirements of the claim(s) to which it refers, adding its own additional requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine what a dependent claim covers, look at both the dependent claim and the claim(s) to which it refers. The instruction suggests it may be helpful to submit a chart showing dependencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's role in claim construction and jury's role in application
rubrics_metrics.description: The law says that it is the court's role to define the terms of the claims and it is the jury's role to apply the court's definitions to the issues being decided. You must accept the court's definitions of claim terms as correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court's definition of claim language should not be taken as an indication of the court's view regarding infringement or invalidity. For any claim words the court has not defined, the jury should apply the ordinary meaning (as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art). Authorities such as Markman and Phillips are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: For claim terms without court definitions use ordinary meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claim term for which the court has not provided you with a definition, you should apply the ordinary meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'ordinary and customary meaning' is based on the understanding of a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention; the jury must apply the court's provided constructions and otherwise use ordinary meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition phrase meanings in claim drafting (comprising/consisting/consisting essentially of)
rubrics_metrics.description: The instructions explain usage: 'comprising' is open-ended and allows additional elements; 'consisting of' is closed and means 'I claim what follows and nothing else'; 'consisting essentially of' is a middle ground between open-ended and closed-ended language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authoritative case law examples are provided to illustrate how courts interpret these transition phrases when construing claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office Action and examiner findings
rubrics_metrics.description: After the prior art search and examination of the application, the Examiner informs the applicant in writing of what the Examiner has found and whether the Examiner considers any claim to be patentable and thus would be 'allowed.' This writing from the Examiner is called an 'Office Action.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Examiner rejects the claims the applicant may respond and try to persuade the Examiner to allow the claims or amend/submit new claims; the exchange can continue until allowance, final rejection, or appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury's ultimate tasks summarized
rubrics_metrics.description: Your job will be to decide whether or not claims [ ] of the [ ] patent have been infringed and whether or not those claims are invalid. If you decide that any claim has been infringed and is not invalid, you will then need to decide any money damages to be awarded and whether any infringement was willful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The summary frames the sequential determinations the jury must make (infringement by claim, invalidity defenses, damages, willfulness) and notes differing burdens/standards for different issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 112, paragraph 6 (means-plus-function / step-plus-function) applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the asserted claims include means-plus-function or step-plus-function requirements, Section 112, paragraph 6 applies (instruction provided only where such claims are at issue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This instruction is flagged to be included only when means-plus-function claim elements are at issue; the full text of how to apply §112, ¶6 appears later in the instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims as the primary source for scope, rest of patent as context
rubrics_metrics.description: The figures and text in the rest of the patent provide a description and/or examples of the invention and provide a context for the claims, but it is the claims that define the breadth of the patent’s coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specification/drawings to understand claim terms where appropriate, but remember the claims set the legal boundaries.
